opus-5.5.text:
I think the greatest value wasn't any single course. It was the environment, and the standard it set for me.

When you're surrounded by classmates who are extremely talented, many of them with medals from the International Olympiad in Informatics or other competitions, you very quickly lose any illusion that you're special just because you're good at math or programming. That was humbling, and honestly a bit painful at first. But it forced me to ask a more important question: if I'm not going to be the best at the thing everyone else is competing on, what is the thing I actually care about and can do differently?

For me, that turned out to be computer graphics and physical simulation. I spent a lot of time building things on my own, writing renderers and simulators, often outside what was required for class. The Yao Class gave me the freedom and the foundation to do that. The theoretical training in algorithms and mathematics was very rigorous, and even though I ended up in a more systems-and-graphics direction, that rigor stayed with me. When you design a programming language or a compiler for simulation, you constantly rely on that way of thinking.

The other big value was exposure. We had opportunities to go abroad for research, to meet people working at the frontier, and to see what world-class research looks like up close. That really expanded my sense of what's possible. Before that, publishing at a top venue or doing a PhD at MIT felt like something distant. After that, it felt like something you could actually work toward step by step.

So if I had to summarize it: the Yao Class gave me solid fundamentals, a very high bar, and, maybe most importantly, the push to find my own path instead of just following the crowd.

r001.rationale: The response names the peer environment and the high standard set by exceptionally talented classmates as the greatest value of Yao Class, while also describing other benefits.

r002.rationale: It says his talented classmates made him question whether he was special, but does not state that this showed him how many remarkable people there are in the world.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the greatest value wasn't any particular course. It was the people. When I got into Yao Class, I quickly realized that pretty much everyone around me was smarter than me in some dimension. There were people who could solve algorithm problems I couldn't even parse, people who'd been doing competition math since they were ten. That's humbling at first, but it recalibrates what you think is normal. You stop asking "can this be done" and start asking "how fast can we do it."

The second thing is that the environment gave us a very solid theoretical foundation while also leaving us a lot of freedom. Professor Yao designed the curriculum around theory, algorithms, complexity, that kind of thing. But nobody told you what to do with your time outside of class. So I spent a lot of time just building things, writing renderers, playing with graphics and simulation, basically for fun. I don't think I'd have had that combination anywhere else, where you're forced to be rigorous but also trusted to go explore.

And the third thing, which I only appreciated later, is that it taught me taste. When you're surrounded by people doing really good work, you develop a sense of what a good problem looks like versus what's just busywork. A lot of what I did afterward at MIT, and then with Taichi, came from that instinct of picking problems that are both technically deep and actually useful to somebody. I think that instinct was formed in those four years, mostly from watching my classmates and arguing with them late at night in the dorm.

r001.rationale: He says the greatest value was the people and describes his classmates as exceptionally capable.

r002.rationale: He says his classmates recalibrated what seemed normal, but does not clearly state that this made him realize how many remarkable people there are in the world.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I think the greatest value was learning how to approach difficult problems. The Yao Class gave me a strong foundation in computer science, but more importantly, it encouraged me to look beyond a particular technique and ask why something works and whether there’s a better way.

Being surrounded by curious, talented classmates was also a big part of that experience. You encounter different ways of thinking, and that pushes you to question your own assumptions. For me, the lasting value is that foundation and the confidence to explore something unfamiliar and learn what I need along the way.

r001.rationale: The response says talented classmates were a big part of the experience, but identifies learning to approach difficult problems as the greatest value; it does not name classmates as the greatest gain.

r002.rationale: It says classmates exposed him to different ways of thinking, but does not state that this made him realize how many remarkable people there are in the world.

Being surrounded by curious, talented classmates also pushes you to question your assumptions and explore ideas you might otherwise overlook.
